analysis.one_liner: Requires wireless carriers to prorate and cap cell phone early termination fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by four Senate Democrats in December 2009 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Federal Communications Commission to write rules requiring cell phone companies to shrink early termination fees month by month as a contract runs its course, and to cap any fee at what the company actually paid for the customer's phone minus what the customer paid for it. It would also have required companies to disclose the fee clearly at purchase and on monthly bills. The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Cell phone customers who want to switch carriers before their contract ends. Under contracts common at the time, leaving early could cost $150 to $350 no matter how much of the contract remained; the bill would have reduced that penalty each month and tied it to the actual subsidized cost of the handset. It also would have preserved states' ability to set their own stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone customers stuck in contracts

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to write rules that carriers prorate early termination fees over the life of the contract, so the penalty shrinks each month instead of staying fixed [S2][S3].
Caps any early termination fee at the carrier's cost of the handset, minus what the subscriber paid for the phone up front, so customers can no longer be charged more than the company lost [S2][S3].
Requires clear disclosure of the fee at the point of sale and on every monthly bill, showing what the customer would owe if they canceled before the next cycle [S3].
Explicitly preserves state and local laws regulating early termination fees, so states could go further than the federal rule [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers would lose a reliable revenue stream: early termination fees generated billions a year industry-wide and discouraged customers from switching, so carriers would face more churn and weaker lock-in. Carriers could respond by raising handset prices or monthly rates to make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: Carriers and their trade groups argued early termination fees let them subsidize expensive phones — customers paid less upfront for the handset in exchange for the contract — so cutting the fees could mean higher upfront phone prices or monthly rates [S3] (the bill itself directs the FCC to weigh the business rationale for the fees).
The bill directs the FCC to consider the fees' effect on competition, reflecting the carriers' argument that the subsidy model helped customers afford phones and helped smaller carriers compete [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is modest and targeted: it does not ban the fees, it makes them match what the carrier actually lost on the phone and shrink over time. The main cost is that carriers might shift some subsidy recovery into higher prices or upfront phone costs, and the FCC rulemaking could have produced a fee schedule that left some customers little better off. But the current structure penalized switching far beyond the carrier's actual loss, and the bill's disclosure and proration requirements addressed that directly. On balance the benefits to customers outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on December 3, 2009, joined by Sens. Feingold, Webb, and Begich [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wireless carriers keep collecting fixed early termination fees that can far exceed their actual handset loss, and customers who switch carriers early keep paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wireless carriers and their fee revenue

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 3 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Feingold, Webb, and Begich).

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Senate Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits is recorded.

industries.note: Early termination fees were a major source of carrier revenue and a key tool for keeping customers locked into contracts. The bill would have capped the fees at the carrier's actual handset cost and shrunk them monthly, making it cheaper for customers to switch providers.
